idiom_name: Casbin-C++ Enforcer (PERM model.conf + policy.csv) or a SyncedEnforcer on the concurrent request path
implementation_notes: The Apache Casbin C++ port (casbin-cpp) supplies the whole model: declare the request/policy/role-link shape in a model file (m = g(r.sub, p.sub) && r.obj == p.obj && r.act == p.act with [role_definition] g = _, _), keep subject->role and role->permission rows in a policy file or adapter, and call Enforce({sub, obj, act}) at the decision point; GetImplicitRolesForUser exposes the hierarchy closure and the RBAC API adds/removes roles and permissions at runtime. Because the plain Enforcer is not thread-safe, a multi-threaded server uses SyncedEnforcer (a shared_mutex around policy reads and reloads) or wraps an Enforcer itself. Projects unwilling to take the dependency hand-roll the four relations as std::unordered_map<std::string, std::set<Permission>> plus a role-hierarchy graph closed transitively at load time, making the decision a set-membership test with std::string_view keys that allocate nothing per request. Either way the enforcement seam is one guard function or middleware called from every entry point, and the subject is the verified principal - never a value pulled from the request.
pitfalls: The plain Enforcer is not thread-safe; sharing one across request threads without SyncedEnforcer or a shared_mutex races policy reads against reloads and grant/revoke writes.
Rebuilding the Enforcer per request reloads the policy from disk; keep one instance per process and reload on a watcher or signal.
A hand-rolled hierarchy must be closed transitively once at load time - a per-request recursive walk is both slow and a stack-overflow vector on a cycle.
Storing the subject's roles in a token and trusting it keeps a revoked role alive until expiry; resolve roles server-side from the policy store.
Map lookups keyed by a temporary std::string allocate on every check; key on std::string_view into stable storage.
